title: Reliable and Safe Trustworthy Software Architectures

slides.title: Reliability Requirements for AI-Native Pipelines
bullets: Correctness: outputs match specification
Robustness: graceful handling of unexpected inputs
Performance: latency and throughput bounds
Reproducibility: deterministic results across runs
Maintainability: clear contracts and low coupling
Security: protection against injection and leakage
slides.notes: Introduce the six core reliability requirements that any AI‑native testing pipeline must address. Emphasize that these requirements are not independent; a design decision often trades off one against another. Relate each requirement to concrete pipeline stages (generation, testing, evaluation, deployment).

slides.title: Automated Testing Pipeline Stages
bullets: Specification capture (requirements, contracts)
Code generation (LLM or agent)
Static analysis (lint, type check, security scan)
Dynamic testing (unit, integration, contract, property‑based)
Stress & mutation testing for robustness
Evaluation & selection (metrics, thresholds)
slides.notes: Walk through each stage, highlighting where AI‑specific nondeterminism appears (generation, dynamic testing). Note that static analysis is deterministic and can catch many defects early, while dynamic stages must be designed for flakiness mitigation.

slides.title: Specification‑Driven Development for AI Code Generation
bullets: Formal specs (pre/post conditions, invariants) guide generation
Specs become executable contracts for testing
Reduces ambiguity between human intent and model output
Enables automated verification of generated code
Supports traceability from requirement to test
slides.notes: Explain how specification‑driven development (SDD) structures the prompt and the evaluation harness. Cite the 2026 SDD paper (C2) which shows that explicit specs improve both correctness and reproducibility of generated artifacts.

slides.title: AlphaCode Competition Pipeline Case Study
bullets: Problem parsing → natural language to formal spec
Large‑scale candidate generation (millions of programs)
Filtering by syntax and static checks
Clustering by output behavior on generated tests
Evaluation on held‑out test suite (generated + hidden)
Selection of top‑k submissions for final ranking
slides.notes: Describe the AlphaCode pipeline accurately: it parses the problem, generates massive numbers of candidates, filters and clusters them, then evaluates using both generated and held‑out tests before selecting a submission. This illustrates how correctness, performance, and reproducibility are addressed at each stage (C1).

slides.title: Complexity Backpressure as a Policy for AI Agents
bullets: Definition: reject or refactor generated code exceeding complexity thresholds
Configurable token‑budget limits per module
Modularity metrics (cyclomatic complexity, depth)
Integrated as a gate in the static analysis stage
Not a universal standard; a course‑proposed policy
slides.notes: Present complexity backpressure as the course’s proposed policy for controlling overly complex AI‑generated code. The 2026 cross‑model study (C3) shows that token and modularity thresholds reduce downstream debugging effort, but they are configurable checks, not an industry standard.

slides.title: Assessing a Multi‑Component Pipeline Design
bullets: Scenario: three services (API, ML model, data prep) with shared contract
Requirement list: correctness, robustness, reproducibility, maintainability
Design decision 1: contract tests at service boundaries → correctness & maintainability
Design decision 2: property‑based tests on ML outputs → robustness
Design decision 3: deterministic seed & versioned data for ML → reproducibility
Design decision 4: complexity backpressure gate on generated glue code → maintainability
Justify each decision against at least one requirement
slides.notes: Walk through the worked problem step by step, showing how to map each pipeline design decision to explicit reliability requirements. This demonstrates the assessment skill required for CO4.LO2 (Bloom level 5). Encourage students to practice with their own project milestones.

slides.title: Contract Testing for Service Interfaces
bullets: Verifies provider/consumer compatibility
Runs against a shared contract (OpenAPI, gRPC proto)
Detects breaking changes early in CI
Primary reliability target: correctness of integration
Secondary benefit: maintainability through explicit contracts
slides.notes: Explain contract testing as a specialized integration test that validates interface compliance. It directly supports correctness by catching mismatched schemas, and indirectly aids maintainability by making contracts first‑class artifacts (C4).

slides.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for Context Exchange
bullets: MCP standardizes tool, resource, and context exposure
Clients request context; servers provide typed resources
Does not itself adjust context windows or perform retrieval
Context selection and token‑budget policies are client‑side
Improves traceability when versions and execution settings are controlled
slides.notes: Clarify that MCP is a protocol for exchanging context and invoking tools, not a built‑in context‑tuning mechanism. The 2026 query‑tuning framework (C5) uses MCP to standardize the context supplied to an agent; reproducibility gains come from the client controlling retrieval, versioning, and execution parameters.

slides.title: Query Tuning via MCP in a Testing Workflow
bullets: Test harness requests relevant schema via MCP
Agent receives versioned contract and data samples
Client enforces token budget and deterministic retrieval
Generated tests are executed in a sandboxed runner
Results logged with full context provenance for replay
slides.notes: Illustrate a concrete workflow where MCP standardizes the context fed to a test‑generation agent. By fixing the context version and token budget, the pipeline achieves better traceability and reproducibility, consistent with the query‑tuning framework (C5).

slides.title: Check: Reliability Requirement Identification

quiz.question: Which reliability requirement is primarily addressed by static analysis gates (lint, type checking, security scans) in an AI‑native pipeline?
quiz.explanation: Static analysis detects defects and violations before execution, directly supporting correctness. While it can also catch some robustness issues, its primary purpose is to ensure the generated code conforms to language rules and specified contracts, i.e., correctness.

slides.notes: Use this quick poll to confirm students distinguish correctness (static guarantees) from robustness (runtime behavior). The most tempting distractor is robustness because static analysis can flag unchecked error paths, but the core target is correctness.

slides.title: Check: Pipeline Design Decision Justification

quiz.question: Contract testing of service interfaces primarily verifies which reliability requirement for AI‑native pipelines?
quiz.explanation: Contract testing ensures that provider and consumer implementations honor the same interface specification, directly guaranteeing integration correctness. Maintainability is a secondary benefit because contracts become explicit documentation, but the primary verification target is correctness.

slides.notes: Reinforce that contract testing’s main goal is correctness of integration. Maintainability appears as a distractor; clarify that while contracts aid maintenance, the test itself validates correct behavior.

slides.title: Hands‑On Reliability Assessment Lab
bullets: Clone the provided multi‑component repo (API, ML, data prep)
Run the existing CI pipeline and collect test reports
Identify gaps against the six reliability requirements
Propose two concrete pipeline improvements with justifications
Submit a short markdown report via the course portal
slides.notes: Students work in pairs on their development machines using the AI coding tools from the lab (week 11). They practice the assessment skill from CO4.LO2 by mapping observed pipeline stages to reliability requirements and proposing justified enhancements. Instructor circulates to answer questions.

slides.title: Flakiness Mitigation in AI‑Generated Tests
bullets: Quarantine flaky tests and rerun with fixed seeds
Use deterministic test data and mock external services
Apply statistical thresholds (e.g., 95% pass rate over 10 runs)
Log environment hashes for reproducibility
Integrate flakiness dashboard into CI
slides.notes: Summarize practical strategies from the autonomous coding agents study (C6) to reduce nondeterministic test failures. Emphasize that flakiness undermines reproducibility and correctness guarantees, so systematic mitigation is essential in AI‑native pipelines.

slides.title: Ensuring Reproducibility via Controlled Reruns
bullets: Pin model versions, prompts, and temperature settings
Version control all generated artifacts and test inputs
Use containerized execution environments
Record full provenance (context, seed, dependencies)
Enable on‑demand replay for audit and debugging
slides.notes: Detail concrete steps to achieve reproducibility, drawing on AlphaCode’s evaluation methodology (C1) and the complexity backpressure study (C3). Controlled reruns turn nondeterministic generation into an auditable process, supporting both reproducibility and correctness.

Metrics: error rate, latency percentiles, drift detection
Automated rollback tied to reliability thresholds
Continuous evaluation loops feed back into pipeline
Project milestone due: integrated pipeline demo

slides.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Six reliability requirements guide every pipeline decision
Specification‑driven development and contract testing anchor correctness
Complexity backpressure and flakiness mitigation protect maintainability and reproducibility
MCP standardizes context exchange; reproducibility comes from client‑side controls
Assessment skill: map design choices to explicit requirements with justification
slides.notes: Conclude by recapping the main themes: requirements‑driven design, concrete AI‑native testing stages, and the assessment mindset needed for the project milestone and final exam. Remind students to review the lab report feedback.
